gloss: The space above the earth that you see when you look up.
examples: The *sky* turned orange right before the storm hit.
There wasn't a cloud in the *sky* all week.
Clear *skies* are in the forecast through Sunday.

gloss: A white or gray mass of water droplets floating in the sky.
examples: A dark *cloud* moved in over the lake.
The *clouds* finally broke around noon.
You could see his breath turn into a little *cloud* of steam.

gloss: The star that the earth goes around and that gives us light and heat.
examples: The *sun* comes up around six this time of year.
Don't sit in the *sun* too long without a hat.
Some of those planets orbit two *suns*.
contrast: *Sun* and *son* are perfect homophones in American English.

gloss: The large round object that circles the earth and shines at night.
examples: There's a full *moon* tonight.
The *moon* was so bright we didn't need a flashlight.
Jupiter has dozens of *moons*.

gloss: A huge ball of burning gas that looks like a point of light at night.
examples: Out in the desert you can see thousands of *stars*.
That bright *star* is actually Venus.
We lay on the roof and counted *stars*.

gloss: The light and warmth that come directly from the sun.
examples: We got two straight weeks of *sunshine*.
The kitchen gets great *sunshine* in the morning.
After all that rain, the *sunshine* felt amazing.

gloss: Natural light from the sun.
examples: Keep the paint out of direct *sunlight*.
*Sunlight* was pouring through the blinds.
These plants need about six hours of *sunlight* a day.

gloss: The light that comes from the moon at night.
examples: We walked back to the cabin by *moonlight*.
The snow looked blue in the *moonlight*.
There was just enough *moonlight* to see the trail.

gloss: A narrow line of light or heat traveling from something.
examples: A *ray* of sun came through the curtains.
Sunscreen blocks the *rays* that burn your skin.
The first *rays* hit the top of the mountain.

gloss: An area that is cooler and darker because something blocks the sun.
examples: Let's eat in the *shade* — it's ninety degrees out here.
That old oak gives the whole yard *shade*.
There's no *shade* anywhere on this beach.
contrast: Russian «тень» splits in two: *shade* is the cool area out of the sun, *shadow* is the dark shape an object casts.

gloss: The dark shape made on a surface when something blocks the light.
examples: My *shadow* was ten feet long by five o'clock.
The *shadows* got longer as the sun went down.
He stepped out of the *shadow* of the building.

gloss: The moment the sun appears above the horizon in the morning.
examples: We were on the road before *sunrise*.
That was the best *sunrise* I've seen all summer.
The park opens at *sunrise* and closes at dark.

gloss: The moment the sun goes down below the horizon in the evening.
examples: The *sunset* over the water was unbelievable.
Be back at the dock by *sunset*.
People come out here just for the *sunsets*.

gloss: The first light of the day, just before the sun comes up.
examples: The crew starts work at *dawn*.
We drove all night and got there at *dawn*.
It was a cold, gray *dawn*.

gloss: The dim light at the end of the day, just after sunset.
examples: The deer come out around *dusk*.
We played ball until *dusk*.
The streetlights come on at *dusk*.

gloss: The soft half-light in the sky before sunrise or after sunset.
examples: We hiked the last mile in *twilight*.
In summer the *twilight* lasts almost an hour up here.
The lake looked silver in the *twilight*.

gloss: The natural light of day, or the hours when it is light outside.
examples: We only have about two hours of *daylight* left.
The colors look completely different in *daylight*.
Try to get off the mountain while there's still *daylight*.

gloss: The time when it gets dark at the end of the day.
examples: They wanted to reach the campground by *nightfall*.
The temperature drops fast after *nightfall*.
The search was called off at *nightfall*.

gloss: The line where the sky seems to meet the land or the sea.
examples: A storm was building on the *horizon*.
You could just see a ship on the *horizon*.
The sun dropped below the *horizon* at 8:14.
contrast: The stress falls on the middle syllable — huh-RY-zuhn, not HOR-i-zon.

gloss: An event in which one body in space blocks the light of another.
examples: Schools closed early so kids could watch the *eclipse*.
There's a lunar *eclipse* next Tuesday night.
Total solar *eclipses* are rare in any one place.

gloss: A statement of what the weather is expected to be.
examples: The *forecast* says rain all weekend.
Did you check the *forecast* before you packed?
These ten-day *forecasts* are never right.

gloss: The usual weather a place has over many years.
examples: Arizona has a dry *climate*.
My knees do better in a warm *climate*.
These grapes only grow in cool *climates*.

gloss: The layer of gases surrounding a planet.
examples: Most meteors burn up in the *atmosphere*.
The upper *atmosphere* is far colder than that.
Mars has a thin *atmosphere* with almost no oxygen.
contrast: Stress the first syllable — AT-muhs-feer, unlike Russian «атмосфЕра».

gloss: One of the four parts of the year, or a period with typical weather.
examples: Fall is my favorite *season*.
We get all four *seasons* here.
Hurricane *season* runs from June through November.

gloss: A unit for measuring temperature.
examples: It's supposed to hit ninety *degrees* tomorrow.
The temperature dropped twenty *degrees* in an hour.
Water freezes at thirty-two *degrees* Fahrenheit.

gloss: The amount of water vapor in the air.
examples: It's not the heat, it's the *humidity*.
The *humidity* makes my hair frizz.
August here is ninety degrees with eighty percent *humidity*.

gloss: Small amounts of water in the air, in the ground, or on a surface.
examples: There's still *moisture* in the soil from last night.
The bag keeps *moisture* out.
Wipe the *moisture* off the windows before it freezes.

gloss: Water that falls from the sky as rain, snow, sleet, or hail.
examples: We've had almost no *precipitation* since April.
Expect some *precipitation* by Thursday evening.
Annual *precipitation* here is about forty inches.

gloss: How far you can see, given the weather conditions.
examples: *Visibility* was down to about a hundred feet.
Flights were delayed because of poor *visibility*.
The fog lifted and *visibility* improved.

gloss: An instrument that measures air pressure to help predict weather.
examples: The *barometer* is falling, so expect a storm.
My grandfather had a brass *barometer* by the door.
*Barometers* were standard equipment on every ship.

gloss: A scientist who studies and predicts the weather.
examples: The *meteorologist* on Channel 4 got it right for once.
*Meteorologists* had been tracking the storm for days.
She trained as a *meteorologist* before going into TV.

gloss: The boundary between two masses of air, which usually brings a change in weather.
examples: A cold *front* is moving in tonight.
The *front* stalled over the valley and it rained for three days.
Warm *fronts* usually bring steady rain instead of thunderstorms.
contrast: Spelled with an o but pronounced FRUNT, rhyming with *hunt*.

gloss: A period of violent weather with strong wind and usually rain or snow.
examples: We lost power during the *storm*.
A big *storm* is supposed to come through Friday night.
Three *storms* hit the coast in two weeks.

gloss: A storm with thunder and lightning, usually with heavy rain.
examples: A *thunderstorm* rolled through and knocked out the internet.
The dog hides under the bed during *thunderstorms*.
Afternoon *thunderstorms* are normal here in July.

gloss: The loud noise you hear after a flash of lightning.
examples: The *thunder* woke up the whole house.
You could hear *thunder* off in the distance.
Count the seconds between the flash and the *thunder*.
contrast: *Thunder* is uncountable: say "we heard thunder" or "a clap of thunder", never "a thunder".

gloss: A bright flash of electricity in the sky during a storm.
examples: *Lightning* hit a tree in the neighbor's yard.
Get off the water when you see *lightning*.
There was *lightning* but almost no rain.
contrast: Spelled *lightning*, with no e — *lightening* is a different word meaning "making lighter". It is also uncountable: "a bolt of lightning", not "a lightning".

gloss: A short period of rain or snow.
examples: We got a quick *shower* around lunchtime.
Scattered *showers* are likely this afternoon.
The *shower* passed in about ten minutes.

gloss: Very light rain made of fine drops.
examples: It's just *drizzle* — you don't need an umbrella.
The game went on through a steady *drizzle*.
Cold *drizzle* is somehow worse than real rain.

gloss: A sudden, very heavy fall of rain.
examples: We got caught in a *downpour* on the way to the car.
The *downpour* flooded the intersection in minutes.
Two *downpours* in one afternoon washed out the trail.

gloss: A single drop of falling rain.
examples: The first *raindrops* hit the windshield.
A fat *raindrop* landed right on my nose.
*Raindrops* were beading up on the fresh wax.

gloss: The amount of rain that falls in a place over a period of time.
examples: *Rainfall* was well below average last year.
Heavy *rainfall* overnight closed two roads.
The county measures *rainfall* at six different stations.

gloss: A curved band of colors in the sky, caused by sun shining through rain.
examples: There was a huge *rainbow* over the field after the storm.
We saw a double *rainbow* from the porch.
*Rainbows* show up whenever the sun comes out during rain.

gloss: A small pool of water left on the ground after rain.
examples: The kids went straight for the biggest *puddle*.
Watch out — that *puddle* is deeper than it looks.
There were *puddles* all over the parking lot.

gloss: Small balls of ice that fall from storm clouds.
examples: *Hail* the size of quarters dented every car on the lot.
We pulled over and waited out the *hail*.
The storm brought wind, rain, and *hail*.
contrast: *Hail* is uncountable — one piece of it is *a hailstone*, never "a hail".

gloss: A single ball of ice that falls during a hailstorm.
examples: A *hailstone* cracked the skylight.
Some of the *hailstones* were as big as golf balls.
He picked up a *hailstone* and held it in his palm.

gloss: Frozen or partly frozen rain that falls in cold weather.
examples: The rain turned to *sleet* around midnight.
Driving in *sleet* is worse than driving in snow.
There was *sleet* on the steps and I almost went down.

gloss: Snow that has partly melted into a wet, dirty mush.
examples: The sidewalks were nothing but gray *slush*.
My boots are soaked from all that *slush*.
By noon the snow had turned to *slush*.

gloss: A single piece of falling snow.
examples: A *snowflake* landed on her glove and melted.
Big wet *snowflakes* were coming down fast.
No two *snowflakes* are supposed to be alike.

gloss: A storm in which a lot of snow falls, usually with wind.
examples: The *snowstorm* shut down every school in the county.
We drove home through a *snowstorm* at fifteen miles an hour.
Two *snowstorms* in one week is a lot, even for here.

gloss: An occasion when snow falls, or the amount that falls.
examples: The first *snowfall* of the year came in October.
We had a heavy *snowfall* overnight.
*Snowfalls* like that used to happen every winter.

gloss: A severe snowstorm with strong wind and very poor visibility.
examples: The *blizzard* dumped two feet of snow on the city.
They were stuck at the airport for two days because of the *blizzard*.
My parents still talk about the *blizzard* of '78.

gloss: A brief, light fall of snow.
examples: We're expecting *flurries* tonight, nothing serious.
A *flurry* blew past the window and stopped.
There were *flurries* on the drive up, but nothing stuck.

gloss: A deep pile of snow formed by the wind.
examples: There's a *snowdrift* halfway up the garage door.
The plows left *snowdrifts* at the end of every driveway.
He stepped into a *snowdrift* and sank to his knees.

gloss: A ball of snow packed together in your hands.
examples: He threw a *snowball* at his brother and missed.
The snow's too dry to make *snowballs* today.
One *snowball* hit the window and everybody froze.

gloss: A figure of a person built out of packed snow.
examples: The kids built a *snowman* in the front yard.
Our *snowman* lasted about three days.
There were *snowmen* on half the lawns on the street.
contrast: Irregular plural: one *snowman*, two *snowmen* (SNOH-men).

gloss: A pointed piece of ice hanging down where water has frozen as it dripped.
examples: There's a three-foot *icicle* hanging off the gutter.
Knock those *icicles* down before somebody gets hurt.
An *icicle* broke off and shattered on the steps.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A thin white layer of ice crystals, or a night cold enough to form one.
examples: There was *frost* on the windshield this morning.
The first hard *frost* killed the tomatoes.
Late *frosts* can ruin the whole apple crop.

gloss: A period of warmer weather when snow and ice melt.
examples: We got a *thaw* in the middle of January.
The river floods every spring during the *thaw*.
A couple of *thaws* turned the yard into mud.

gloss: Drops of water that form on cool surfaces outdoors overnight.
examples: The grass was still wet with *dew*.
Wait for the *dew* to burn off before you mow.
There was *dew* all over the tent by morning.
contrast: Americans say DOO, a homophone of *do* and *due*; the British say DYOO.

gloss: Injury to the skin and flesh caused by extreme cold.
examples: He got *frostbite* on two fingers.
Cover your ears or you'll risk *frostbite*.
At that wind chill, *frostbite* sets in within minutes.

gloss: A thick cloud of water droplets near the ground that makes it hard to see.
examples: The *fog* was so thick I couldn't see the mailbox.
*Fog* rolls in off the bay almost every morning.
The bridge was closed because of *fog*.

gloss: A thin fog, or a fine spray of tiny water drops in the air.
examples: There was *mist* hanging over the river at sunrise.
A light *mist* was falling, barely enough to wet the road.
The *mist* burned off by nine o'clock.

gloss: A slight cloudiness in the air from dust, smoke, or heat.
examples: There's a *haze* over the whole valley from the wildfires.
You could barely make out the skyline through the *haze*.
Summer *haze* makes the mountains look blue.

gloss: Dirty, unhealthy air over a city, made of smoke and fog.
examples: The *smog* was bad enough that they told kids to stay inside.
You can see the *smog* sitting over the freeway.
*Smog* here is much worse in the summer.

gloss: A form of oxygen that forms a protective layer high in the atmosphere.
examples: The *ozone* layer blocks most of the sun's harmful rays.
*Ozone* at ground level is a pollutant, not a good thing.
They issued an *ozone* alert for the whole metro area.

gloss: Fine powder from plants that floats in the air in spring.
examples: The *pollen* count is through the roof this week.
There's yellow *pollen* all over my car.
My eyes water whenever the *pollen* gets bad.

gloss: Air moving across the land or the sea.
examples: A cold *wind* was coming off the lake.
The *wind* took my hat halfway down the block.
*Winds* of forty miles an hour knocked out the power.
contrast: The noun is WIND (rhymes with *pinned*); the verb *to wind* a clock is WYND (rhymes with *find*).

gloss: A light, pleasant wind.
examples: There's a nice *breeze* on the porch.
The *breeze* off the ocean keeps it from getting too hot.
Evening *breezes* make August almost bearable.

gloss: A sudden strong rush of wind.
examples: A *gust* blew the umbrella off the table.
*Gusts* up to sixty miles an hour are expected.
One good *gust* and the whole tent came down.

gloss: A very strong wind.
examples: A *gale* was blowing straight off the water.
The forecast has *gales* along the whole coast.
They canceled the ferry because of the *gale*.

gloss: A very large, violent tropical storm with extremely strong circling winds.
examples: The *hurricane* is expected to make landfall Thursday.
They boarded up the windows before the *hurricane*.
Three *hurricanes* hit the Gulf that season.
contrast: Stress the first syllable, HUR-uh-kayn, and pronounce the last syllable fully — unlike Russian «ураган».

gloss: A hurricane that happens in the western Pacific.
examples: The *typhoon* forced them to cancel the flight.
A *typhoon* had wiped out the docks the year before.
*Typhoons* are most common there in late summer.

gloss: A large system of winds spinning around a center of low pressure.
examples: A *cyclone* was forming off the coast.
The *cyclone* brought a week of rain.
Tropical *cyclones* get their energy from warm ocean water.

gloss: An informal American word for a tornado.
examples: A *twister* took the roof clean off the barn.
They spotted a *twister* about two miles out.
*Twisters* come through this county every spring.

gloss: A seasonal wind that brings months of heavy rain.
examples: The *monsoon* usually starts in early July.
They lost the crop when the *monsoon* came late.
*Monsoons* dump most of the region's yearly rain.

gloss: How cold the air feels on your skin once the wind is taken into account.
examples: It's ten degrees, but the *wind chill* makes it feel like twenty below.
Watch the *wind chill* before you send the kids out.
The *wind chill* was the story on every newscast that night.

gloss: An unpleasant feeling of cold in the air or in your body.
examples: There's a *chill* in the air tonight.
Grab a jacket — you'll catch a *chill* out there.
The morning *chill* is gone by ten.

gloss: A stretch of unusually hot weather lasting several days or more.
examples: We're in the middle of a *heat wave*.
The *heat wave* broke on Sunday night.
Two *heat waves* in one summer is unusual for Seattle.

gloss: A short period of unusually cold weather.
examples: That *cold snap* in April killed the blossoms.
We're getting a *cold snap* this weekend.
A couple of *cold snaps* like that and the pipes will freeze.

gloss: The pleasant quality of being warm.
examples: You could feel the *warmth* coming off the sidewalk.
We stepped inside for a little *warmth*.
Wool keeps its *warmth* even when it's wet.

gloss: A long period with little or no rain.
examples: The *drought* has lasted three summers now.
Farmers lost most of the corn to the *drought*.
*Droughts* out west are getting longer and hotter.
contrast: Despite the gh, it is pronounced DROWT and rhymes with *out* — not "drawt" or "druft".

gloss: A large amount of water covering land that is usually dry.
examples: The *flood* took out the bridge on Route 9.
They're still cleaning up after the *flood*.
*Floods* like that used to happen once a century.
contrast: The oo here is /ʌ/: *flood* rhymes with *blood* and *mud*, not with *food*.

gloss: A large fire that spreads quickly through forest or grassland.
examples: The *wildfire* burned forty thousand acres.
Smoke from the *wildfires* reached us three states away.
A dry summer makes a *wildfire* much more likely.

gloss: A mass of snow and ice sliding suddenly down a mountainside.
examples: An *avalanche* closed the pass for two days.
The *avalanche* risk is high after that much fresh snow.
*Avalanches* are the main danger on that route.

gloss: A dangerous condition caused by the body getting far too hot.
examples: Two runners were treated for *heatstroke*.
Never leave a dog in the car — *heatstroke* happens fast.
Dizziness and confusion are warning signs of *heatstroke*.

gloss: Red, sore skin caused by too much time in the sun.
examples: I got a nasty *sunburn* on the boat.
His *sunburn* peeled for a week.
*Sunburns* that bad can do real damage.
contrast: Americans usually say "I got *a* sunburn", counting it; the British more often say "I got sunburn", with no article.

gloss: A huge mass of ice that moves very slowly down a valley.
examples: The *glacier* has pulled back half a mile since the sixties.
You can hike right up to the edge of the *glacier*.
Most of these *glaciers* will be gone in fifty years.
contrast: Americans say GLAY-shur; the British say GLASS-ee-ur.

gloss: A large piece of ice floating in the sea, broken off from a glacier.
examples: We passed an *iceberg* the size of a house.
Most of an *iceberg* sits below the waterline.
The ship changed course to avoid the *icebergs*.

gloss: The season between winter and summer, when plants start to grow.
examples: We're putting the house on the market in the *spring*.
*Spring* came early this year.
The last three *springs* have been unusually wet.

gloss: The warmest season of the year, between spring and fall.
examples: We spend every *summer* at my aunt's place.
It was the hottest *summer* on record.
She waited tables for three *summers* to pay for school.

gloss: The season between summer and winter, when leaves change color.
examples: The leaves are beautiful here in the *fall*.
She starts law school this *fall*.
We've had some cold *falls* lately.
contrast: Americans normally say *fall*; the British say *autumn*. Both are understood in the US.

gloss: The season between summer and winter; the more formal American word for fall.
examples: The poem is set in late *autumn*.
*Autumn* in New England draws tourists from everywhere.
He painted the same hillside over several *autumns*.
contrast: The final n is silent: AW-tuhm. It comes back only in the adjective *autumnal* (aw-TUM-nuhl).

gloss: The coldest season of the year, between fall and spring.
examples: *Winter* here lasts about five months.
We got through the *winter* on firewood alone.
He's lived through sixty Minnesota *winters*.

gloss: Either of the two days in the year with the longest or shortest daylight.
examples: The summer *solstice* falls on June 21st this year.
After the winter *solstice* the days start getting longer.
The stones line up with the sun on both *solstices*.

gloss: Either of the two days a year when day and night are about equal in length.
examples: The fall *equinox* is around September 22nd.
Storms are common near the *equinox*.
The two *equinoxes* mark the start of spring and fall.

gloss: A large round body in space that moves around a star.
examples: Mars is the fourth *planet* from the sun.
There are eight *planets* in our solar system.
They think that *planet* may have water.

gloss: The planet we live on.
examples: The *earth* takes a year to go around the sun.
From orbit you can actually see the curve of the *earth*.
It's the only place on *earth* where those birds nest.

gloss: The earth seen as a whole, or a round model of it.
examples: The company has offices all over the *globe*.
There was a dusty *globe* on the teacher's desk.
Old *globes* still show countries that don't exist anymore.

gloss: All of space and everything in it.
examples: The *universe* is still expanding.
Nobody knows how big the *universe* actually is.
Some physicists argue for a whole set of parallel *universes*.

gloss: A huge group of stars, gas, and dust held together by gravity.
examples: Our *galaxy* has a few hundred billion stars.
The telescope picked up *galaxies* nobody had seen before.
That smudge of light is another *galaxy*.

gloss: A body of ice and dust that travels around the sun and grows a bright tail.
examples: The *comet* should be visible just after sunset.
That *comet* only comes back every seventy-six years.
*Comets* pick up their tails as they get close to the sun.
contrast: Don't confuse it with the verb *commit*: the noun is KAH-mit, stressed on the first syllable; *commit* is kuh-MIT.

gloss: A piece of rock from space that burns as a streak of light in the sky.
examples: We saw a *meteor* go right across the sky.
The *meteor* shower peaks around two in the morning.
You can count twenty *meteors* an hour out here.

gloss: A piece of rock from space that reaches the ground without burning up.
examples: A *meteorite* punched a hole in somebody's garage roof.
The museum has a *meteorite* you're allowed to touch.
Most *meteorites* found on earth are mostly iron.

gloss: A small rocky body that orbits the sun, much smaller than a planet.
examples: An *asteroid* passed closer to us than the moon.
Most *asteroids* sit in a belt between Mars and Jupiter.
They named the *asteroid* after her.

gloss: The curved path one object takes around another in space.
examples: The satellite is in a low *orbit*.
The moon's *orbit* isn't a perfect circle.
It completes sixteen *orbits* a day.

gloss: An object placed in orbit around a planet, or a moon that orbits naturally.
examples: The weather *satellite* sends back new images every ten minutes.
We get our internet by *satellite* out here.
There are thousands of *satellites* up there now.

gloss: A group of stars that people picture as forming a shape.
examples: That *constellation* is easy to find in winter.
My dad taught me a few *constellations* when I was a kid.
The app tells you which *constellation* you're looking at.

gloss: The curved shape of the moon when only a thin part of it is lit.
examples: There was a thin *crescent* low in the western sky.
The moon was down to a *crescent* by the end of the week.
He drew two *crescents* on the chalkboard.
contrast: The sc in the middle is a single /s/ sound: KRES-uhnt, not "kres-KENT".

gloss: An instrument that makes distant objects look closer, used for looking at the sky.
examples: He got a *telescope* for his twelfth birthday.
You need a *telescope* to see the rings of Saturn.
The observatory has two big *telescopes*.

gloss: The scientific study of stars, planets, and space.
examples: She's taking *astronomy* as an elective.
*Astronomy* got a lot easier once we had good telescopes.
There's a great *astronomy* club at the community center.
contrast: Don't mix it up with *astrology* (uh-STRAH-luh-jee), the business of horoscopes — *astronomy* is the science.

gloss: A scientist who studies stars, planets, and space.
examples: An *astronomer* at the university spotted it first.
*Astronomers* have been arguing about that for decades.
She's an *astronomer* who works mostly with radio telescopes.

gloss: A person trained to travel and work in space.
examples: Every kid in that class wanted to be an *astronaut*.
The *astronauts* spent six months on the station.
A retired *astronaut* came to speak at the school.

gloss: A vehicle built to travel in space.
examples: The *spacecraft* docked without any trouble.
Two unmanned *spacecraft* are already on the way.
The *spacecraft* sent back photos for eleven years.
contrast: The plural does not change: one *spacecraft*, three *spacecraft* — like *aircraft*.

gloss: A vehicle or device pushed upward by burning fuel, used to reach space.
examples: The *rocket* lifted off right on schedule.
They're testing a new *rocket* next month.
Those *rockets* can be flown back and reused.

gloss: The force that pulls objects toward each other, and things toward the earth.
examples: *Gravity* on the moon is about a sixth of what it is here.
You don't notice *gravity* until you try to carry something heavy.
Their bones weaken without *gravity*.

gloss: A round hole in the ground made by an impact or an explosion.
examples: You can see individual *craters* on the moon with binoculars.
The meteorite left a *crater* fifty feet wide.
The whole surface is covered in *craters*.

gloss: A building with telescopes, used for studying the sky.
examples: The *observatory* is open to the public on Friday nights.
They built the *observatory* on top of the mountain.
Several *observatories* tracked the same object.

gloss: One half of the earth, divided north and south or east and west.
examples: It's winter here and summer in the southern *hemisphere*.
That plant only grows in the northern *hemisphere*.
The seasons are reversed between the two *hemispheres*.

gloss: Bands of colored light that appear in the night sky near the poles.
examples: We drove north hoping to see the *aurora*.
The *aurora* was green with streaks of purple.
Strong solar storms can push *auroras* much farther south.

gloss: A star together with all the planets and other bodies orbiting it.
examples: Neptune is at the far edge of our *solar system*.
The kids built a model *solar system* out of foam balls.
They've found thousands of other *solar systems*.

gloss: The distance light travels in one year, used for measuring space.
examples: That star is about four *light-years* away.
One *light-year* is close to six trillion miles.
The galaxy is a hundred thousand *light-years* across.
contrast: It measures distance, not time, even though the word *year* is in it.

gloss: A region in space with gravity so strong that not even light can escape it.
examples: There's a *black hole* at the center of our galaxy.
Nothing that falls into a *black hole* comes back out.
*Black holes* form when very large stars collapse.
